0.title: God's Good Design for Body and Desire
0.essay:
Few subjects are more confusing or painful in our culture than sexuality. The Bible says something better than both the world’s message and the church’s embarrassed silence.

Two failures

The modern West tells people that their sexual desires define who they are, that consent is the only moral boundary, and that any limit on sexual expression is oppression. Many Christians, meanwhile, have heard the church speak about sex mainly in terms of rules and shame, or not at all.

A gift first

Scripture begins not with prohibitions but with a gift. God made us male and female and called his creation “very good” (Genesis 1:31). He designed sexual union as a profound joining of husband and wife. Sex is not dirty or shameful. It is so precious that God has placed it within the protective boundaries of marriage, and so meaningful that it points beyond itself to Christ’s love for his church (Ephesians 5:31–32).

Truth and compassion

This study tries to hold truth and compassion together. It speaks clearly about God’s design, because God’s design is good and his commands are for our flourishing. It speaks gently, because every reader is a sinner, many carry deep wounds, and some are wrestling with desires they did not choose. The gospel has good news for all of them.

The chapters

God’s Good Design; Purity in a Broken World; The Gift of Singleness; Same-Sex Attraction; Male and Female He Created Them; and Healing, Forgiveness and Hope. The study belongs alongside those on Christian Marriage, Biblical Manhood and Biblical Womanhood.

For reflection

Has your view of sex been shaped more by the culture around you, by shame, or by Scripture?

1.title: God's Good Design
1.essay:
The Bible’s teaching on sexuality begins in a garden, with a wedding. Before there was any sin to warn against, there was a gift to celebrate.

Male and female

“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Our sex as male or female is not an accident or a mere social construction. It is part of how God made us, and men and women bear his image equally. Neither alone tells the whole story.

The difference between the sexes is not a problem to be overcome but a gift to be received. And straight away God blessed them and gave them a task: to be fruitful and multiply, and to rule the earth on his behalf (Genesis 1:28). Sexual difference is woven into God’s purpose for the world.

Made for each other

In Genesis 2 we see the same story up close. God said, “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him” (Genesis 2:18). Adam named the animals, but none was a fitting partner. God’s answer was not another man but a woman. He made her from the man and brought her to him, like a father walking his daughter down the aisle. Marriage was God’s idea, and he was its first witness.

Adam responded with a song of delight: “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23). Man and woman are alike enough to be partners, and different enough to complete each other.

One flesh

Then comes the founding statement of marriage: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Here is the pattern: leaving, holding fast, becoming one. Sexual union is the physical expression of a whole-life covenant. It joins two people at the deepest level, which is why it belongs only within marriage. Everything Scripture later says about sexuality builds on this verse.

Without shame

“And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25). Before the fall there was perfect openness and trust. Sex was a delight without fear, guilt or exploitation.

Jesus affirms the design

When the Pharisees tried to trap Jesus with a question about divorce, he took them back to the beginning: “Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female” (Matthew 19:4). He then quoted Genesis 2:24 and concluded, “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (Matthew 19:6). For Jesus, God’s creation design is the norm for marriage and sexuality. Marriage is not a human invention to be redefined at will. It is God’s work.

Delight in marriage

The Bible is not embarrassed by sexual pleasure in marriage. When a father in Proverbs warns his son against adultery, he does not make sex sound bad. He makes faithfulness sound wonderful: “rejoice in the wife of your youth” and “be intoxicated always in her love” (Proverbs 5:18–19). The best protection against sexual sin is delight in God’s good gift. The Song of Songs celebrates married love in poetry, and Paul tells married couples not to deprive one another (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). God is the inventor of sexual joy.

Think of a young Christian couple, both raised in churches that only spoke about sex as something to avoid. In their marriage they struggle with guilt. Reading Genesis 2 and Proverbs 5 together, they realise that God is not embarrassed by their union. He designed it. Slowly, their shame begins to lift.

The purposes of sex

Scripture shows several purposes for sexual union in marriage. There is union: the two become one flesh. There is procreation: “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28). There is delight (Proverbs 5:18–19). And there is protection against temptation (1 Corinthians 7:2–5). These purposes belong together within the covenant of marriage.

A picture of Christ

Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and then says, “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). Marriage, including its sexual union, is a living picture of Christ’s covenant love for his people. That is why God guards it so carefully.

The body matters

Christianity never treats the body as unimportant. God made it. Christ took a body. The Spirit dwells in it. And it will be raised (1 Corinthians 6:13–14). What we do with our bodies matters to God.

For reflection

Do you think of sexuality mainly as God’s good gift or mainly as a problem? What would change if you began, as Scripture does, with the gift?

2.title: Purity in a Broken World
2.essay:
The fall damaged every part of human life, including sexuality. Since Eden, desire has been marked by lust, exploitation, betrayal and confusion. Into that broken world God calls his people to purity.

Shame enters

The moment Adam and Eve sinned, “the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked” (Genesis 3:7). The openness of Eden gave way to hiding. Every person since has been affected. No one comes to this subject untouched.

God’s will is your holiness

Paul is direct: “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor” (1 Thessalonians 4:3–4). Christians are not to live “in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God” (1 Thessalonians 4:5).

Sexual immorality covers all sexual activity outside marriage between a man and a woman: sex before marriage, adultery, pornography and other sexual sins. And Paul adds a sober note. To reject this teaching is not to reject a human opinion: “whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you” (1 Thessalonians 4:8).

Purity of heart

Jesus took the commandment against adultery to the heart: “everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). Purity is not only about what we do but about what we desire and dwell on. Jesus then calls for radical action: whatever causes you to sin, cut it off (Matthew 5:29–30). Purity requires both a changed heart and practical decisions about what we look at and where we go.

This is why pornography is so destructive. It trains the heart to treat people as objects. It feeds fantasy. It is often deeply addictive. And behind the screen are real people, many of them exploited.

Your body belongs to the Lord

In Corinth, a city known for its sexual licence, some believers argued that what they did with their bodies did not matter. Paul answered, “The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body” (1 Corinthians 6:13). Sexual union joins two people as one flesh, so sexual immorality joins a member of Christ to sin.

His command is short: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). Not debate with it, not see how close you can get, but run. And the motive is profound. The believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

Marriage honoured

“Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous” (Hebrews 13:4). Notice “among all.” Single people honour marriage by keeping sex for it. Married people honour it by keeping faith within it. God takes sexual sin seriously because he takes marriage seriously.

Why consent is not enough

Our culture tends to treat consent as the only rule. Consent is essential: without it, sexual activity is abuse. But God’s design asks for more than consent. It asks for covenant: a lifelong, exclusive promise in which sexual union expresses total self-giving. Two people agreeing to something does not make it good.

God’s boundaries also protect the vulnerable. Sexual sin harms not only individuals but families, children and whole communities, and it is so often women and children who bear the cost.

Practical purity

For single people, purity means saving sex for marriage, and in dating, treating the other person as a brother or sister in Christ. Living together before marriage, even without sex, puts people in the way of temptation and blurs the meaning of marriage. For married people, purity means faithfulness of body and heart, guarding against emotional affairs, and treating one’s spouse with honour. For everyone, it means wisdom with screens, friendships and situations.

Think of an engaged Christian couple whose friends tell them it is unrealistic not to live together before the wedding. They decide to wait. It is hard. But on their wedding day they have the joy of beginning their life together with nothing hidden and nothing regretted.

Purity is not perfection

No one is perfectly pure. Every Christian has impure thoughts and desires to fight. Purity is a direction of life, not a flawless record, and it is pursued by grace, not by willpower alone. When we fall, we confess, receive forgiveness and get up again.

For reflection

What is the biggest threat to your sexual purity right now? What is one practical step you can take this week to guard against it?

3.title: The Gift of Singleness
3.essay:
Many churches unintentionally treat singleness as a waiting room or a problem to be fixed. Yet Jesus was single. Paul was single. And Scripture speaks of singleness not as second best but as a good gift.

Paul’s view

Paul writes, “I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another” (1 Corinthians 7:7). He sees both marriage and singleness as gifts. Neither is spiritually superior. He tells the unmarried and widows that it is good for them to remain single, though it is not wrong to marry.

He even points out particular advantages of singleness. The married person rightly cares about pleasing a spouse. The single person can be anxious about the things of the Lord and serve him with undivided devotion (1 Corinthians 7:32–35). Paul is not trying to restrict anyone, but to promote devotion to Christ.

Jesus’ view

When the disciples heard Jesus’ high standard for marriage, they said it might be better not to marry. Jesus spoke of those who remain unmarried for different reasons, including those who do so “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.” And he said, “Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matthew 19:12). Singleness for the sake of the kingdom is an honourable calling.

Is singleness a special gift?

Some read 1 Corinthians 7:7 as meaning that only those with a supernatural absence of sexual desire should remain single. More likely, Paul means that whatever state a person is in, married or single, is God’s gift for that time. Singleness is a gift whenever God gives it, even when it is not wanted.

Not a lower calling

Some traditions have treated celibacy as spiritually higher than marriage. Others treat marriage as the normal mark of adulthood and maturity. Both are wrong. Each is a calling from God, with its own joys and burdens.

Marriage is for this age

Jesus said that “in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30). Human marriage is a signpost. The ultimate marriage is between Christ and his church, and single Christians already belong to it. Their lives are a reminder that human marriage is not the final goal of life. No one is incomplete because they are unmarried. Paul says of every believer, “you have been filled in him” (Colossians 2:10). Christ, not a spouse, is the source of our wholeness.

Jesus himself lived as a single man, fully human and fully whole. He had deep friendships: “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus” (John 11:5). His life shows that a single life can be full of love, friendship and purpose.

The church as family

In Israel, eunuchs could have no children and were excluded from parts of temple worship. Yet God promised those who kept his covenant “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5). In God’s family, no one is left out because of their marital status. “God settles the solitary in a home” (Psalm 68:6). And Jesus said, “whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Mark 3:35).

The church must be a real family for single people. That means including them in homes, holidays and leadership, not treating them as incomplete or always seating them at the “singles” table. Think of a woman in her forties who has never married and often feels invisible at church, where most events are built around couples and families. Then a family invites her to Sunday lunch every week. Their children call her “aunt.” She mentors younger women and leads a Bible study. Her singleness has not been taken away, but it is no longer lonely.

The struggles of singleness

Many single people did not choose singleness and long to be married. That longing is not sinful, and they may freely pray for a spouse. But they also face loneliness and sexual temptation without the gift of marriage. They need honesty, friendship and support, not pat answers. Paul himself said, “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11). Contentment is learned, not instant, and it is learned in company.

For reflection

How does your church treat single people: as family, or as people waiting for real life to begin? If you are married, which single person could you welcome into your home this month? If you are single, how can you honestly bring your longings to God while finding contentment in Christ?

4.title: Same-Sex Attraction
4.essay:
This is one of the most painful and debated questions facing the church today. It is not an abstract issue. It concerns real people, including Christians in our own churches, who experience same-sex attraction, often from a young age, and who did not choose it. They deserve both truth and love.

What Scripture says

The Bible consistently describes sexual relationships between people of the same sex as contrary to God’s design. The Law forbids them (Leviticus 18:22). In Romans 1, Paul describes how humanity exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshipped creation rather than the Creator. God’s judgment was to give people up to their desires: “For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature” (Romans 1:26), and men did the same (Romans 1:27).

In 1 Corinthians 6:9–10, men who practise homosexuality are listed with the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers and swindlers among those who will not inherit the kingdom. Every biblical reference to same-sex sexual activity is negative, and every biblical description of marriage is between a man and a woman.

Not a worse sin

Notice the company this sin keeps. In 1 Corinthians 6 it stands alongside greed, drunkenness and slander. Same-sex activity is not singled out as uniquely terrible. Christians who are proud of their own heterosexual purity while ignoring their greed or gossip have misunderstood the gospel. And Romans 1 leads straight into Romans 2 and 3, where Paul shows that all are guilty. The passage is about all of us before it is about anyone else.

Such were some of you

Paul’s list in 1 Corinthians 6 turns on one small word: were. “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). The church in Corinth was a mixed community of former idolaters, adulterers, thieves, drunkards and those who had practised homosexuality. Paul did not tell them to clean themselves up first. He said they had been washed. Their past did not define them; their Saviour did.

Attraction and action

Experiencing same-sex attraction is a result of living in a fallen world, as all our disordered desires are. Feeling a temptation is not the same as sinning. A believer who experiences same-sex attraction and resists it out of love for Christ is walking faithfully.

Such attractions may or may not change in this life. Some people experience change; many do not. God does not promise that the desires will disappear. But he promises grace to live faithfully, and a future in which every desire will be made whole. Jesus himself “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). So believers who face this temptation have a high priest who understands, and they can come to the throne of grace to “find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). And “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability” (1 Corinthians 10:13). Faithfulness is possible, not by our strength, but by his.

The views

Some Christians today argue that the biblical texts addressed only exploitative forms of same-sex activity, such as the abuse of boys or temple prostitution, and that faithful, committed same-sex relationships are acceptable. The historic view of the church, in every tradition and century, is that same-sex sexual relationships are contrary to God’s will.

The historic view is right. Romans 1 grounds its teaching not in exploitation but in creation: the exchange of natural relations for what is “contrary to nature.” Jesus defined marriage by the creation pattern of male and female (Matthew 19:4–6). And Scripture never presents any same-sex sexual relationship positively.

Identity

A Christian’s deepest identity is not their sexual attractions but their union with Christ. Christians disagree over language, such as whether to describe oneself as a “gay Christian.” It is wise to avoid language that suggests our desires define who we are. But all should speak with gentleness, remembering that every believer’s desires are disordered in some way.

The church’s calling

Pressure, shaming, or coercive programmes promising to change orientation have caused great harm. The church’s task is to proclaim the gospel, call everyone to faithfulness, and walk patiently with those who struggle. Churches must be places where believers who experience same-sex attraction can be honest without fear of rejection or gossip, where they find deep friendship and family, and where they are supported in faithfulness. Many such believers have chosen celibacy for Christ, often at great cost. They should be honoured, not pitied.

Think of a young man in a church youth group who realises he is attracted to other young men. Terrified, he tells no one for years. Finally he confides in his pastor, expecting rejection. Instead his pastor thanks him for his trust, assures him of God’s love, opens the Bible with him and promises to walk with him. He finds a few close friends in the church who know his story and stand with him. His struggle is real, but he is no longer alone.

For reflection

If someone in your church confided that they experience same-sex attraction, would they find in you both truth and love? How does 1 Corinthians 6:11 bring hope to every sinner, including you?

5.title: Male and Female He Created Them
5.essay:
Our culture increasingly teaches that a person’s gender is set by an inner sense of identity rather than by the body. The Bible gives a different foundation, and it calls us to hold it with great compassion.

A real struggle

Some people experience gender dysphoria: a deep and painful distress that their body does not match their sense of who they are. This is a real and often agonising experience. Those who face it are not projects to be fixed but people to be loved, and they deserve great compassion.

The body is a gift

God made us as embodied beings. David marvels: “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:13–14). Our bodies are not random. They are crafted by God with care and purpose.

From the beginning, the two sexes are woven into the account of creation: God made humanity in his image, and “male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). To be human is to be embodied as male or female. Our sex is something we receive, not something we choose. It is part of creation’s original goodness, not a later imposition.

Living in a fallen world

Because of the fall, our bodies and minds do not always work as God designed. Some people are born with conditions in which physical sex is unclear. Some experience deep distress about their sex. These are not chosen, and they are not a reason for shame. They are part of the brokenness that affects all creation.

Paul is honest about that brokenness: “we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now” (Romans 8:22). Believers groan too. Those who struggle with their bodies share in this groaning, and in its hope.

Receiving our bodies

The Christian response to gender distress is not to reshape the body to fit an inner sense of self, but to seek healing and peace in receiving the body God has given, while walking patiently with the distress. This is hard, and it may take a lifetime. It requires deep pastoral care, wise counsel and a loving church family.

Paul says that the believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Those words were written about sexual purity, but they also shape how we view our bodies: as gifts entrusted to us, to be used for God’s glory, not possessions to be remade at will.

The views

Some argue that gender identity, not the body, determines whether a person is a man or a woman, and that affirming a person’s inner identity, including through medical transition, is the most loving response. The historic Christian view is that God gives our sex through our bodies, and that we are called to receive it.

The historic view is right. Scripture grounds our identity as male or female in creation (Genesis 1:27; Matthew 19:4) and in the body. Altering the body to deny one’s sex rejects the goodness of God’s design. Yet compassion must govern how we speak and act.

Stereotypes are not Scripture

In Scripture, men and women are not interchangeable (Deuteronomy 22:5; 1 Corinthians 11:14–15). Yet much of what our culture calls masculine or feminine is merely cultural. A gentle boy who loves art, or an adventurous girl who loves climbing trees, is not in the wrong body. Churches should avoid narrow stereotypes that make children feel they are not “real” boys or girls.

Children and teenagers

Parents and churches should respond to a child’s confusion with patience and love, not panic, avoiding both harsh reactions and quick affirmation of a new identity. For many young people, the distress eases over time.

Think of a Christian family whose teenage daughter tells them she believes she is a boy. Shocked, they are tempted to react with anger. Instead, they listen, tell her they love her, and seek wise Christian counsel. They do not affirm a new identity, but they do not reject her. Over several years, with much prayer, patience and support, she comes to peace with her body. Her parents know other stories may end differently, and they pray for every family facing this.

Mercy for those who have transitioned

People who have undergone transition and later come to Christ need a church that welcomes them, helps them walk forward faithfully, and never treats them with contempt. The Ethiopian official in Acts was a eunuch, a man whose body had probably been altered, and who would have been excluded from the temple assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1). Yet Philip told him the good news about Jesus and baptised him at once (Acts 8:35–38). Isaiah’s promise to eunuchs was being fulfilled. Christ welcomes those whose bodies bear the marks of a broken world.

The hope of resurrection

Our bodies will be raised and transformed. “We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). And “the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18). Everyone who has struggled with their body has this hope: a body made whole.

For reflection

When this subject comes up, is your first reaction anger, fear or compassion? How can you hold firmly to God’s design while showing real love to those who struggle?

6.title: Healing, Forgiveness and Hope
6.essay:
No one comes to this subject with clean hands. Every person reading this has sinned sexually, in deed, in thought, or both. Many have also been sinned against. The gospel is good news for the guilty and for the wounded.

Forgiveness for the guilty

King David committed adultery and arranged a murder to cover it up. When he repented, God forgave him (2 Samuel 12:13; Psalm 51). There is no sexual sin the blood of Christ cannot cleanse. God’s invitation still stands: “though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18).

Luke tells of a woman known in her town as a sinner who entered a Pharisee’s house and wept over Jesus’ feet, wiping them with her hair. The Pharisee was scandalised. Jesus told a parable about two debtors and said, “her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much” (Luke 7:47). Then he spoke to her directly: “Your sins are forgiven” (Luke 7:48), and “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:50). Jesus welcomes the sexually broken.

Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho. She hid the Israelite spies and trusted in Israel’s God. She was spared, joined God’s people, and became an ancestor of King David and of Jesus himself (Matthew 1:5). Her past did not disqualify her from grace.

Healing for the wounded

Sexual abuse is a horrific evil. Those who have been abused bear no guilt for what was done to them. The guilt belongs entirely to the abuser. Yet victims often carry a deep shame that is not theirs to carry.

Christ, who was himself stripped and shamed on the cross, understands. The God who “determines the number of the stars” is the same God who “heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (Psalm 147:3–4). His greatness and his tenderness belong together. Healing may take years, and wise counsel and medical help may be needed. But the God of all comfort is near. And any abuse must be reported to the proper authorities.

Guilt and shame

Guilt is the objective fact of having sinned. Shame is the feeling of being unclean or unworthy. Christ deals with both. He bears our guilt on the cross, and he removes our shame by clothing us in his righteousness: “he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10). The one who has been sinned against needs that covering as much as the one who has sinned.

A new identity

In Christ, a person’s past does not define them. “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The adulterer, the addict, the survivor of abuse, and the one who struggles with lifelong temptation are all invited to find their identity in Christ.

Rebuilding

Forgiveness does not remove every consequence. A forgiven adulterer may still face divorce. A forgiven abuser must still face the law. God’s forgiveness is complete, but some earthly consequences remain, and grace is present even in them.

After sexual sin, rebuilding trust in a marriage takes time, honesty and often outside help. After addiction, freedom involves accountability and practical change. After abuse, healing involves safety, truth and patient care. Think of a married man who confesses to his wife that he has been viewing pornography for years. She is devastated. With the help of their pastor and a Christian counsellor, he takes practical steps towards freedom and accountability. It takes over a year for trust to begin to return. Today their marriage is stronger and more honest than before, and they both know it was grace.

The church as a hospital

The church should be a place where sexual sin and sexual wounds can be confessed and healed, not hidden. That requires both clear teaching and deep compassion. A church that has only one of these will either crush people or leave them where they are.

The great wedding

Every human marriage, and every human longing for love, points to a greater reality: the marriage of Christ and his church. “Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7). The Bride is clothed in fine linen, bright and pure. Married or single, every believer is invited to that feast. There every wound will be healed and every longing fulfilled.

For reflection

Is there a sexual sin or wound you have never brought to Christ? He is ready to forgive and to heal. What would it look like to bring it to him today, and perhaps to a trusted friend or pastor?
